points.label: Opening phrase
points.left: Genesis begins, 'In the beginning, God created.'
points.right: John begins, 'In the beginning was the Word.'

points.label: Creation
points.left: God creates heavens and earth and speaks light into the scene.
points.right: All things are said to come into being through the Word.

points.label: Light
points.left: Light is separated from darkness and named day.
points.right: Life in the Word is called the light of people, shining in darkness.

compares.posture: Hold the two openings together without flattening either into the other.

rightEvidence.title: The Word, creation, life, and light appear together

compares.tension: Both passages begin with creation language, but Genesis names God creating while John distinguishes God and the Word and says all things came through the Word.

leftEvidence.title: Humanity is created in God’s image and blessed

points.right: The narrative narrows to one formed human before the garden is described.

points.right: Formation and received breath are central.

points.right: The human is materially formed from the ground.

compares.posture: Read the broad human commission beside the close-up formation scene.

rightEvidence.title: The man is formed from dust and receives breath

leftEvidence.title: Humanity receives image, blessing, and rule

points.right: Humans are described as placed over the works of God’s hands.

edges.basis: Hold the two openings together without flattening either into the other. Both passages begin with creation language, but Genesis names God creating while John distinguishes God and the Word and says all things came through the Word.
edges.label: Beginning / beginning

edges.basis: Read the broad human commission beside the close-up formation scene. Genesis 1 speaks of humanity collectively as male and female; Genesis 2 narrows to one human formed from dust and animated by breath.
edges.label: Humanity spoken / human formed

edges.basis: Notice what Psalm 8 keeps from Genesis and what changes when the same human role is expressed as wonder. Genesis commissions humanity within creation, while Psalm 8 turns the same small-yet-honored place into a question of wonder.
edges.label: Commission / wonder

edges.basis: Hold the first seventh day beside the later command that explicitly remembers it. Genesis describes God finishing and resting; Exodus turns that completed pattern into a command governing Israel’s recurring work and rest.
edges.label: Rest / remembered rest

edges.basis: Read the creation statement first, then observe how Hebrews places it inside a larger argument. Genesis locates rest at the completion of creation, while Hebrews still speaks of a rest open to enter.
edges.label: Finished rest / continuing rest

edges.basis: Notice recognizably shared images without assuming the two settings are identical. Eden’s river waters a garden with named lands, while Revelation’s river flows from the throne through a city with healing and unending light.
edges.label: Garden river / final river

edges.basis: Let the two passages provide different scales of description. Genesis 1 presents male and female together within the human commission, while Genesis 2 narrates formation, recognition, and one flesh at close range.
edges.label: Male and female / one flesh

edges.basis: Observe the sequence of perception, covering, fear, and hiding before moving to later consequences. The pair is naked and unashamed before the rupture, then covers and hides after listening, seeing, taking, and eating.
edges.label: Unashamed / covered and hidden

edges.basis: Notice Jeremiah’s reuse of creation vocabulary without turning the prophecy into a second creation account. Genesis moves from an unformed opening toward order, while Jeremiah reuses unformed and empty language for devastation.
edges.label: Formless opening / devastated reversal

edges.basis: Compare form as well as content: declarative narration beside divine questions. Genesis narrates divine ordering directly; Job voices the same foundations and sea boundaries through questions that expose human absence and limits.
edges.label: Creation narrated / creation questioned

edges.basis: Compare the world coming into order with the world continuing to operate. Genesis presents the world coming into ordered fullness, while Psalm 104 praises that world as continually watered, fed, and inhabited.
edges.label: Beginning / ongoing world

edges.basis: Hold two different literary pictures of water being bounded. Genesis divides and gathers waters through command, while Job pictures the sea as a newborn shut behind doors and bounded by decree.
edges.label: Separated waters / bounded sea

edges.basis: Notice the repeated breath/life relationship while respecting the different scales of the two passages. Genesis describes one human receiving breath and becoming alive, while Psalm 104 describes many creatures dying and being renewed when Spirit is sent.
edges.label: Breath gives life / Spirit renews life

edges.basis: Let the two endings face each other without reducing Revelation to a simple reversal diagram. Genesis ends with the tree of life guarded after exile, while Revelation presents tree, river, throne, healing, and open service in the city.
edges.label: Guarded life / open life

edges.basis: Paul explicitly echoes the creation command when describing illumination in human hearts. Genesis narrates light entering the created order; Paul reuses that speech for inward knowledge without identifying the two events.
edges.label: Light spoken / light in hearts

edges.basis: Genesis assigns lights their work; Psalm 19 turns the heavens and sun into praise without retelling the whole sequence. The lights order signs and seasons in Genesis, while the psalm emphasizes witness, reach, and the sun’s course.
edges.label: Lights assigned / sun celebrated

edges.basis: The first blessing of living creatures can be read beside the psalm’s account of creature dependence on divine breath. Genesis commands abundance; the psalm holds abundance beside death, renewed breath, and continuing dependence.
edges.label: Creatures blessed / creatures dependent

edges.basis: The creation of land animals belongs beside God’s questions about providing for lions and ravens. Genesis reports that land creatures are made; Job stresses needs and provision that continue after their creation.
edges.label: Animals made / animals provided for

edges.basis: The garden command supplies the immediate boundary that the following eating scene contests. Permission dominates the command before one prohibition; the rupture scene narrows attention to the prohibited tree and its fruit.
edges.label: Permission and boundary / taking and eating

edges.basis: Jesus cites creation’s male-female and joining language when answering a later dispute. Genesis first names human aloneness as not good; Matthew emphasizes the joined pair in a contested marital setting.
edges.label: Aloneness named / joined life remembered

edges.basis: The immediate human rupture can be read beside Paul’s wider account of creation subjected to futility and awaiting freedom. Genesis locates blame, pain, toil, and mortality in one garden scene; Romans gives the whole creation a waiting and groaning voice.
edges.label: Hiding after rupture / creation groaning

edges.basis: God’s questions about commanding morning revisit the ordered relation of light and darkness. Genesis gives a sequence of speech, separation, and naming; Job presses the hearer’s limited knowledge of that order.
edges.label: Morning questioned / first light narrated

edges.basis: Job and Psalm 104 both move between cosmic scale and the needs of living creatures. Job speaks through questions that expose human limits; the psalm speaks through praise that describes provision.
edges.label: Cosmic order and hunger / a world sustained

edges.basis: Psalm 33 compresses creation into divine word, breath, gathered waters, and immediate obedience. The psalm’s summary selects speech and breath from a narrative whose opening also retains darkness, deep, and unformed earth.
edges.label: Creation praised by word and breath / the opening narrated

edges.basis: Personified Wisdom recalls being present when God marked creation’s boundaries. Proverbs speaks through a poetic first-person voice; Genesis narrates God separating and naming without that speaker.
edges.label: Wisdom beside the work / waters divided

edges.basis: Both passages use creation to unsettle human estimates of knowledge and power. Isaiah argues that the Creator has no equal; Job’s questions range across created systems and creature needs.
edges.label: Creator without equal / creation beyond human mastery

edges.basis: Isaiah’s statement about an inhabited earth recalls Genesis’ movement from gathered waters to land and vegetation. Isaiah states a purpose in prophetic argument; Genesis narrates ordered land, seas, and seed-bearing growth.
edges.label: Earth formed to be inhabited / land made habitable

edges.basis: Paul’s speech begins with the world’s Creator and speaks of all nations receiving life, times, and boundaries. Genesis gives humanity image, blessing, and rule; Acts stresses shared ancestry, allotted dwelling, and dependence.
edges.label: Nations located / humanity commissioned

edges.basis: Both sources place present creation beside a future release from corruption, death, and pain. Romans describes hope and groaning before release; Revelation announces a new heaven and earth after former things pass.
edges.label: Creation waits / all things made new

edges.basis: Both texts locate all created things in relation to the preexistent Christ or Word. John opens through life and light in narrative proclamation; Colossians expands across visible, invisible, thrones, and continuing coherence.
edges.label: All things through Christ / all things through the Word

edges.basis: Hebrews compresses creation into a claim about God’s word and unseen origin. Genesis narrates what appears at the opening; Hebrews states how faith understands the visible world’s origin.
edges.label: Worlds framed by God’s word / the beginning narrated

edges.basis: The heavenly elders and the psalmist each make created existence a reason for praise. Revelation concentrates the claim in throne-room acclamation; Psalm 104 traces a sustained world in extensive poetic detail.
edges.label: Creation as reason for worship / creation retold in praise

event.centerRule: God → created world → humanity / Adam / Eve → connected places, actions, Spirit, objects, boundaries, blessings, consequences, tensions, memory, and later new-creation language.

characterAnchors.label: God
characterAnchors.note: God is the primary actor throughout the creation event: creating, speaking, separating, naming, blessing, forming, planting, commanding, resting, and later being remembered as Creator.

characterAnchors.label: Adam
characterAnchors.note: The human focus narrows to the man formed from dust, placed in the garden, given work and command, joined to the woman, and later sent from Eden.

characterAnchors.label: Eve
characterAnchors.note: The woman is formed and brought to the man, becomes central to the one-flesh scene, and remains a focal human character in the immediate rupture that follows.

characterAnchors.label: Humanity
characterAnchors.note: Genesis 1 presents humanity collectively as male and female, made in God’s image, blessed, and commissioned within the created world.

event.throughline: God is the primary actor in the creation event. The narrative moves from an unformed opening to ordered regions, living creatures, humanity, rest, and a close human focus in Eden. Adam, Eve, and humanity become focal characters within what God has made. Later Scripture repeatedly returns to creation for praise, command, argument, worship, judgment, and hope.

topic.orientation: Do not turn Creation into a list of doctrines or a debate on arrival. First watch the event itself: who acts, what is spoken, what is separated, named, blessed, formed, placed, commanded, completed, and later remembered. Let Genesis 1–2 remain distinct literary movements while later Scripture reopens their language from different vantage points.
